newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Two old foes in bitter Nicaraguan election fight.
newsitem.headline: Two old foes in bitter Nicaraguan election fight.

text.p: A right-wing populist and the leader of Nicaragua's former Marxist government wound up a bitter election campaign on Wednesday running neck-and-neck in the race for president.

Polls show the left-wing candidate, former Sandinista President Daniel Ortega, narrowing the gap with his pro-business rival Arnoldo Aleman of the Liberal Alliance. The two old foes cast each other as throwbacks to bygone days of dictatorship and civil war.
Ortega has shed the military fatigues and communist dogma that made him an enemy of the United States in the 1980s and has gained on Aleman by picturing himself as a moderate.
Campaigning officially ended on Wednesday under Nicaraguan electoral law.

In a rain-soaked rally in Managua's central plaza, Aleman, the portly former mayor of the capital, sought to give a last-minute boost to his flagging campaign. "On Oct. 20 at the ballot box we will have the last great chance to go forward and escape from the abyss that the dictatorships sank us in," he told an estimated 35,000 red-shirted supporters.

Aleman, a fierce anti-Sandinista who was jailed during Ortega's government in the 1980s, painted the Sandinista as a dictator who would throw Nicaragua back to the "dark night" of its blood-stained past.
"We must shut our ears to the false promises of the old and fierce wolves now disguised as sheep. There is neither mask nor make-up that can hide their failures," Aleman said.

The open enmity of the two main candidates has fuelled fears of renewed polarisation in Nicaragua, which was split by an eight-year war between the Sandinistas and right-wing U.S.-backed Contras in the 1980s that left 25,000 dead.
Aleman has tried to form an anti-Sandinista coalition, bringing together former right-wing Contras rebels and returned exiles who fled Nicaragua during Sandinista rule.

Ortega has equated an Aleman victory to a return to Anastasio Somoza, the right-wing dictator toppled by the Sandinista revolution in 1979 after decades of oppression. He has sought to play down his own revolutionary zeal, saying he supported private enterprise and was keen to build bridges with his former enemy, the United States.
But the new-look Ortega, with contact lenses and a trimmed moustache, has failed to convince the middle-class right.
"I don't believe he's changed. They're still the same bunch of liars as always," said Mariela Fernandez, 21, returning from Miami where her family fled to exile in 1981.
There are 21 other candidates in the race but they draw only a tiny fraction of the vote, reflecting the absence of a political centre in a country still caught in the divisions of the Cold War.

The possibility of a Sandinista victory has worried Nicaraguan businessmen, who have warned of dire economic consequences if Ortega wins. But in one of the poorest countries in the Western Hemisphere, where more than half the population is underemployed or unemployed, Ortega's left-wing roots have continued to strike a chord with the poor.
